procedural_history.originating_court: National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)/National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order passed by the High Court in Criminal Appeal Nos.2305-2307 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos.2302-2303 of 2022, Civil Appeal Nos.793 of 2022, Criminal Appeal No.2298 of 2022, Civil Appeal No.801 of 2022, Criminal Appeal No.2299 of 2022, Civil Appeal No.877 of 2022, Criminal Appeal Nos.2300 And 2304 of 2022 and the order passed by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dated 04.03.2020.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court quashed Section 212(14) direction and the complaint filed by the SFIO, and also quashed and set aside the order passed by the NCLT/NCLAT upholding the proceedings under Section 140(5) of the Act, 2013. The High Court held that the petition filed by the Union of India under Section 140(5) of the Act, 2013 has been satisfied by the subsequent resignation of the auditor and therefore the petition under Section 140(5) of the Act, 2013 filed by the Union of India is no longer maintainable.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached to set aside the judgment and order passed by the High Court, to allow the trial to continue against the accused arrayed in the complaint, and to permit/allow the proceedings under Section 140(5) of the Act, 2013 to be proceeded further so that the NCLT can reach a final conclusion.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of a quasi-judicial tribunal and an inquiry into fraudulent conduct can be overcome or disrupted merely by an act of a party.

facts: An auditor, who was the subject of an inquiry for fraudulent conduct under Section 140(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, resigned from their position.
The argument was made that this resignation rendered the proceedings before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) void and no longer maintainable.
law: The Court examined Section 140(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, which grants the NCLT quasi-judicial powers, similar to a civil court, to investigate and adjudicate on an auditor's fraudulent conduct.
This power is granted 'without prejudice to any action under the provisions of this Act or any other law for the time being in force,' meaning it is an independent power of the Tribunal.
If the NCLT finds that an auditor has acted fraudulently, it can issue a final order, which has serious consequences for the auditor.
application: The Court reasoned that accepting the argument that resignation terminates the inquiry would defeat the entire purpose of Section 140(5).
It would allow an auditor to evade a final order and the consequences of a finding of fraud simply by resigning. The Court stated that this could not have been the intention of the legislature.

Allowing this would mean that the jurisdiction of a quasi-judicial body and an inquiry into serious matters like fraud could be disrupted and frustrated by the unilateral act of a party under investigation.
Therefore, the Court determined that the inquiry must proceed to its logical end, regardless of the auditor's resignation, to ensure the provisions of the law are not rendered ineffective.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that an auditor's resignation cannot overcome the jurisdiction of the NCLT or terminate an ongoing inquiry into fraudulent conduct under Section 140(5). The proceedings are maintainable and must continue to their logical conclusion to prevent auditors from evading the consequences of their actions.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the direction for prosecution under Section 212(14) of the Companies Act, 2013.

facts: The High Court set aside a direction for prosecution issued by the Union of India to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) under Section 212(14) of the Companies Act, 2013.
The High Court's decision was based on two main grounds:
1. The direction to prosecute was issued within 30 hours of the SFIO submitting its report, which the High Court believed demonstrated a non-application of mind.
2. The SFIO report was considered incomplete because investigations into other related subsidiary companies were still ongoing.
law: Section 212(14) of the Companies Act, 2013, empowers the Central Government to direct the SFIO to initiate prosecution based on an investigation report.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning regarding the 30-hour timeframe. It held that the speed of the decision alone cannot be presumed to be a non-application of mind.
The Court stated that the relevant consideration is whether there was sufficient material to prosecute, not the time taken to make the decision.
The Supreme Court also found that the High Court had erred in concluding the report was incomplete. The report was specifically about one company (IFIN) and was complete in that respect.
The fact that investigations into other companies within the larger group (IL&FS) were still ongoing did not render the completed report on IFIN invalid for the purpose of initiating prosecution.
The Court further noted that the accused would have ample opportunity to present their case during the trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had materially erred in setting aside the direction to prosecute. It found the High Court's grounds to be invalid, quashed its judgment, and reinstated the criminal complaint to be proceeded with in the trial court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's observation that relevant facts and documents demonstrating application of mind were not placed on record was correct.

facts: A final order to prosecute was placed on record.
This order specifically stated that the SFIO (Serious Fraud Investigation Office) Report had been reviewed ('having gone through the IFIN SFIO Report').
A detailed note was prepared by an officer and presented to the final authority before the decision to prosecute was made.
The direction to prosecute itself contained details, such as adding more individuals to be prosecuted and correcting a typographical error, which indicated that the report had been considered.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's conclusion was incorrect because there was, in fact, evidence on the record demonstrating the application of mind.
The final prosecution order, which explicitly mentioned a review of the SFIO report, was a key piece of evidence that the High Court overlooked or discounted.
The existence of a detailed note prepared for the final decision-maker showed that a process of review and consideration had occurred.

The Court reasoned that the specific instructions in the prosecution order (to add more accused persons and fix an error) could only have been formulated after a substantive review of the SFIO report, directly contradicting the claim of non-application of mind.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's observation, concluding that it was factually incorrect. The Court pointed to specific evidence on the record—namely the final prosecution order which mentioned a review of the report, the existence of a detailed preparatory note, and the specific, considered instructions within the order itself—as sufficient proof that there had been an application of mind before the decision to prosecute was made.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of a quasi-judicial tribunal and an inquiry into fraudulent conduct can be overcome or disrupted merely by an act of a party.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the resignation of an auditor (the 'act of a party') does not terminate the jurisdiction of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) to inquire into their conduct during their tenure. They contended that allowing resignation to end proceedings would create a loophole for auditors to escape accountability for fraudulent acts.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that the relevant provision of the Companies Act, Section 140(5), applies only to current auditors. They submitted that once an auditor has resigned, they are no longer the 'auditor of the company,' and therefore the NCLT loses jurisdiction to pass an order of removal or debarment against them under that specific section.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the direction for prosecution under Section 212(14) of the Companies Act, 2013.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that the High Court was incorrect to set aside the prosecution. They argued that the direction for prosecution was based on a detailed investigation report and sufficient material evidence, and the decision to prosecute is an executive function that should not be interfered with lightly by the courts.
respondent_arguments: The respondents supported the High Court's decision, arguing that the prosecution was initiated without a proper basis, lacked due application of mind, and was an abuse of the legal process. They maintained that the High Court was correct in quashing such a flawed proceeding.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's observation that relevant facts and documents demonstrating application of mind were not placed on record was correct.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court's observation was factually incorrect. They submitted that the investigation report and all relevant materials were indeed on record and clearly demonstrated that the competent authority had applied its mind before sanctioning the prosecution.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that the High Court's observation was correct. They contended that the appellant had failed to produce the necessary file notings and documents that would have proven that the decision to prosecute was made after a thorough and proper consideration of all facts.

cases.case_name: Madras Bar Association v. Union of India
cases.principle: Apprehension or misuse of the provision in future cannot be ground to test the constitutional validity of the provision.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A jurisdictional fact is a condition precedent to the assumption of jurisdiction by a court, and a court cannot erroneously assume jurisdiction by either not deciding or erroneously deciding the jurisdictional fact.
obiter: Purposive interpretation can be given only when there is some ambiguity in the language of the statutory provisions or it leads to absurd results.
Courts will reject a statutory construction that will defeat the plain intention of the legislature, even if there is some inexactitude in the language used.
A foundational fact must be established before a presumption is made.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The jurisdiction of a quasi-judicial tribunal to conduct an inquiry into fraudulent conduct cannot be overcome or disrupted merely by an act of the party under investigation, such as the resignation of an auditor. Accepting that resignation terminates the inquiry would create a loophole allowing parties to escape accountability, thereby defeating the plain intention of the legislature.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a principle of statutory interpretation that rejects a construction which will defeat the plain intention of the legislature, even if there is some inexactitude in the language used. This purposive approach is favored over a literal interpretation when the latter would lead to an absurd result, such as allowing a party to escape an inquiry into their own fraudulent conduct.
policy_considerations: The court considered that allowing an auditor to avoid an inquiry by resigning would dilute the deterrent effect of the statutory provision designed to prevent fraud.

There is an underlying public policy that an inquiry into fraudulent conduct cannot be considered satisfied or concluded simply by an act of the party being investigated; accountability must be pursued regardless of such actions.
